overview: Kanem, east of Lake Chad, was the earlier heartland of Sayfawa power. Its beginnings remain uncertain; excavated settlements illuminate elite buildings and working materials.

periods.title: An Islamic court and brick settlements
periods.summary: The Sayfawa dynasty ruled an Islamic court. Brick-built elite settlements developed in Kanem, though royal religious affiliation does not date every community’s conversion.

periods.title: Connections across Africa
periods.summary: Imported glass ornaments at Tié reflect connections beyond the Sahara trade. Different glass compositions point to several manufacturing regions; individual finds cannot all be dated to the selected year.

periods.title: A court moves west
periods.summary: Bulala rivalry weakened Sayfawa rule in Kanem. The court’s relocation west of Lake Chad was a political transition, not the disappearance of Kanem’s population.

items.text: At Tié Kalaté S2, discarded bricks lie in a depression where clay was extracted and fired. Nearby residences stood on dunes.
Tié’s substantial enclosure is a candidate for Njimi, the royal capital. The identification remains argued rather than confirmed by a naming inscription.

A study of excavated iron nails distinguishes four main forms used in twelfth- to fourteenth-century Kanem. These ordinary fasteners preserve metalworking choices that monumental buildings alone cannot show. Their precise use must be established from archaeological context.

At Tié, glass dominates the recovered beads, alongside smaller numbers made from ostrich eggshell, metal and stone. Bone pendants and cowries also served as ornaments. This assemblage describes personal adornment at the excavated site, not everyone’s dress.
Many glass beads are tiny cylinders or rounded forms. Makers cut drawn glass and often reheated it to soften sharp edges. Red-brown and yellow shades were common in the recovered collection.

Chemical analysis links a few beads with the glass industry around Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria. Much of the remaining glass has affinities farther east. The results support African exchange connections, while the exact routes and intermediaries remain uncertain.
The Arabic Diwan preserves a royal succession record. Historians compare its chronology with other texts and archaeological dates.
Saharan exchange included enslaved people, horses and cloth. The court’s connections rested partly on coercion as well as commerce.

Cairo was an important meeting point for pilgrims from Kanem and later Borno travelling toward Mecca. Dewière’s study treats pilgrimage as religious practice that also carried people, goods and ideas between African regions.

ending.text: In the late fourteenth century, the Sayfawa court left Kanem for Borno under pressure from Bulala rivals. Kanem continued under other rulers while the dynasty rebuilt its power west of the lake.

sources.title: Carlos Magnavita, Susanne Lindauer and Adoum Casimir Adjbane, New Luminescence and Radiocarbon Dates for Kanem-Borno Fired-Brick Elite Sites (2025)
sources.note: Historical outline and Sites, Materials, and Methods: qualified chronology, brickmaking, settlement interpretation and political change.

sources.title: Sonja Magnavita, Brandi L. MacDonald, Carlos Magnavita and April Oga, Glass beads from Tié (2024)
sources.note: Materials, glass composition and discussion: adornment, manufacturing techniques and probable exchange connections, not a fully reconstructed route.
